note: DRAFT. No in-house lawyer has approved these rules, and until one does every finding produced from this playbook carries playbook_status DRAFT. The thresholds below are ORDINARY MARKET DEFAULTS for an Indian mutual NDA, not this company's standards -- a company that has not written its own playbook does not have one, and pretending otherwise would report a deviation from a standard nobody adopted. Each rule states the standard it encodes so a reviewing lawyer can accept, change or delete it one at a time.
applies_to: Mutual non-disclosure agreements governed by Indian law
not_legal_advice: Every finding is a POTENTIAL_ISSUE against a company standard. Nothing here states what the law requires. Contract Act, Stamp Act and Arbitration Act are not held in this corpus, so no rule below links to them.

rules.why: Confidentiality obligations running longer than three years are hard to administer and are usually negotiated down. Longer terms are common for trade secrets, which is why this is a flag and not a rejection.
An Indian counterparty agreement governed by foreign law makes enforcement slower and more expensive.
Exclusive jurisdiction in a city where the company has no presence turns a small dispute into a travel budget.
An NDA with no definition of what is confidential protects nothing in particular.
The operative promise. Its absence is the single most consequential omission in this document type.
Without a carve-out for disclosure required by law or by a court, the receiving party is promising something it cannot perform.
What happens to the material at the end is the clause people discover is missing at the end.

A non-compete inside an NDA is out of place and is frequently missed because nobody expects to find one there. Code cannot judge whether a particular form is acceptable, so this returns NEEDS_LAWYER rather than a verdict.
Same reason as NDA-08: it changes what the document does, and whether the form is acceptable is a person's call.
An uncapped or very high cap on a mutual NDA is unusual. The figure is an ordinary default and is exactly the kind of number a reviewing lawyer should replace with the company's own.
